parts.note: RE is the formal 'regarding' or 'in the matter of'
pupils address a female teacher as Miss

explanation.surface: A complaint that a teacher has been careless about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With regard to teacher' reads as one phrase, but it splits into two pieces: the formal RE and the schoolroom form of address.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone remiss has failed in a duty through carelessness, so the two words are close synonyms.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the top performance yet achieved
second meaning: a disc of music

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites reading it as praise for one album; really it joins two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A world record is the finest performance ever set, and an LP or vinyl disc of songs is also called a record.

indicators.note: something gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters come out in a bad order

parts.note: the nine letters taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A rueful remark that grave misbehaviour has become everyday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunately' seems a comment on the state of morals, but it tells you to rearrange the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: In Catholic teaching a mortal sin is the gravest category of offence against God, a very serious wrongdoing.

indicators.note: asking whether you said something points at how the word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: broadcast in the sense of sent out, then respelt as a word that sounds identical

explanation.surface: Someone checking whether a music track was played on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' looks like a song on a record; it is the trail an animal leaves, which hounds follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunting dog follows the scent, the smell trail left by its quarry, so scent and track are synonyms in hunting.

clue.text: Dad grabbing an old lady's hat

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece closes around another

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
taken as written
'old lady' is slang for mother, shortened to ma

explanation.surface: Father snatching a hat that belongs to an elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' here is mother, as in 'my old lady'; the 's is read as 'is', the possessive being only surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A Panama is a lightweight brimmed straw hat, so it is a specific example of a hat.

clue.text: Many set free in general pardon

indicators.note: anything freed is released from its fixed place and can fall into a new order

parts.note: the seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Many prisoners released when a government grants a blanket pardon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set free' looks like one phrase about prisoners; 'set' belongs to the letters and 'free' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An amnesty is an official pardon granted to a whole group of offenders at once rather than individually.

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so only every other letter counts

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A famous fighter regularly featured in the popular press.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the even-numbered letters of the newspaper word spells the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Muhammad Ali was a world heavyweight champion and perhaps the most famous boxer of all time.

parts.note: an angle is a point of view or stance
R is the abbreviation for river; 'on' puts it after the other piece

explanation.surface: A fisherman stationed at his spot on the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Position' is not a place on the bank but a viewpoint, as in 'what's your angle?'.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler is someone who fishes with rod and line, the common word for a recreational fisherman.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: exchanging letters with someone

explanation.walkthrough: Two words that look like an adjective and its noun are two separate senses of one participle.
explanation.definitionFit: Corresponding parts match each other, and people who keep up an exchange of letters are said to be corresponding.

indicators.note: something gone off has gone bad or wrong, so the letters spoil into a new order

parts.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A news snippet: officers in China fled the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter makes 'China' look like the country; it is the fine ceramic.
explanation.definitionFit: China is the everyday name for porcelain, the fine white ceramic first made in that country.

clue.text: Criticise a head of state caught in corruption

indicators.note: something caught in a trap sits inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: rot is decay, moral or physical
taken as written

indicators.note: the head of anything is its top, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Attacking a national leader who has been exposed in a graft scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of state' looks like a president; it only means the first letter of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast someone is informal for criticising or mocking them severely.

parts.note: the rest are the others, the remainder
had as in 'had dinner'

explanation.surface: Other people were made to file their accounts a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had to' reads as 'were obliged to'; 'had' is eating and 'to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To restate is to say or declare something once more, which is a fair synonym for reporting again.

clue.text: Coffee from Buffalo Bill country? No

parts.note: Buffalo Bill Cody was a famous figure of the American Wild West
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether some coffee comes from the Wild West, then answering no.
explanation.walkthrough: The final 'No' looks like the answer to the question, but it is just two letters stuck on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An Americano is an espresso diluted with hot water, a standard drink on any cafe menu.

clue.text: Tears prey to pieces for bit of extra fat?

indicators.note: something torn to pieces is broken up, so the letters are scattered and rebuilt

parts.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A predator rips its victim apart to get a fatty morsel.
explanation.walkthrough: A spare tyre is the roll of fat round a person's middle; tyre is the British spelling of tire.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom spare tyre means a roll of flab around the waist, an excess of fat carried like a ring.

parts.note: taken as written
a better is one who is above you, a superior

explanation.surface: Someone acting as an assistant to their boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superior' seems to be the person helped, but it is a synonym for 'better'.
explanation.definitionFit: An abetter assists or encourages someone else, usually in wrongdoing, as in the phrase aiding and abetting.

clue.text: In the morning editor keeps us entertained

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: a.m. stands for ante meridiem, before noon
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor
taken as written

explanation.surface: An editor keeps the newsroom diverted during the morning shift.
explanation.walkthrough: The time abbreviation and the editor abbreviation sit side by side and together hold the pronoun between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To be amused is to be pleasantly diverted, so it swaps directly for entertained as a past participle.

parts.note: to sever is to cut off or detach
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that excluding a European is going too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut off European' looks like a single act against a person; it is a verb followed by an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe weather or pain is very intense, so severe and extreme are close synonyms.

indicators.note: some of a thing is only a part of it, so the answer is a run inside the words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A politician held up a visiting head of state from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first democratically elected president in 1994.

clue.text: The Speaker's delightful set of rooms

indicators.note: whatever a speaker produces is heard rather than read, so the sound matters

parts.note: delightful means charming, then respelt as the identical-sounding word

explanation.surface: The parliamentary Speaker has a charming apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Speaker' looks like the presiding officer of a parliament; it only signals a sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A suite is a connected group of rooms, as in a hotel suite.

clue.text: Polish Republican leaving place of worship

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so a letter departs from the larger word

parts.note: a shrine is a holy place
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A Polish politician walks out of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes 'Polish' look like the nationality; it is the verb to buff.
explanation.definitionFit: To shine shoes is to polish them, so the two verbs mean the same act of buffing.

clue.text: TV show, one that's very like another

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a British satirical puppet series of the 1980s and 90s

explanation.walkthrough: Spitting Image was a British TV comedy that lampooned politicians and celebrities with rubber puppets; fittingly, its puppets were caricature lookalikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone the spitting image of another means they look exactly alike; the idiom also named the British puppet satire.

clue.text: Current prime minister from down under? A troublemaker

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading from under means reading upward, so the letters come back to front

parts.note: PM is the abbreviation for prime minister

explanation.surface: Asking whether the sitting Australian leader is a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From down under' suggests Australia, but in a down entry it means read the piece from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a mischievous little devil, so a naughty child or prankster is called one.

parts.note: de is the French word for from
a port is a harbour

explanation.surface: Throwing someone out of a harbour in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From French harbour' reads as one place; 'from French' translates the preposition and 'harbour' is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: To deport someone is to expel them from a country by legal order, so the verbs are synonyms.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: distant and unfriendly in manner
second meaning: the handset that changes the TV channel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Station controller' sounds like a railway or radio boss; the station is a TV channel and the controller the handset.
explanation.definitionFit: A distant, standoffish person is described as remote, and the handheld device for changing channels is a remote.
